issues.title: [BUG] WaveTools latest changes
issues.body:
@adimako the latest changes to `WaveTools` have introduced a bug where the velocity profile of the waves is not correct (77e6444f08ca36f29b6c955719b3e2f9b0260196). For example, a linear wave with `period=1.`, `mwl=water_depth=1.5`, `height=0.07` will give increasingly high velocities passed a certain depth in the water column.
I also get an OOM error on copper after a while when using `WaveTools` (the error comes faster when using `Fenton` than when using `Linear` waves), I am not sure if it is related to this bug or a separate memory leak.

comments.body:
@adimako, the velocity profiles are mostly fine with 11a46843cc0fcf, but velocities are sharply cut for `d>=lambda/2` for `MonochromaticWaves`.
It did not solve the OOM error problem unfortunately.

@adimako reverting to fd76cd3b4084d93d9e76f95275344488d2710a17 for `WaveTools` (so only the `WaveTools.pyx` file, the rest of proteus on the latest master), the velocity profiles of the waves are different (no cut or increase in velocity for the conditions in the first message above), and it solves the OOM error.
Reverting to the old version is much much slower however, which is expected (4.5+ times slower than the cythonised version for a test case I am running)

@tridelat I do not mind so much the velocity profile, as we can always increase the accuracy of the Taylor approximation possibly to reach lamda = d with acceptable accuracy. The OOM may come from that I am not deallocating memory after function calls. I presume that class is only called once in BC module and not every timestep, so that leaves us with the functions leaking memory. Let me check

The issues with `WaveTools` have now been tackled:
  - **OOM error**: the updates to `WaveTools` that were merged in Proteus 1.2 got rid of the OOM error.
  - **Velocity profile**: The velocity profile can be recovered for the whole water column by using `cosh` and `sinh` instead of `fastcosh` and `fastsinh` at the cost of computational power.
  - **Pressure spikes**: Using `cos` gets rids of pressure spikes that could be encountered when the time step is fine due to approximations of `fastcos` ( @cekees @manuel-quezada )
  - **Water inflow**: Stokes drift velocity that caused the global water level to go up for nonlinear waves can be corrected by subtracting a relevant average velocity from the seabed to the mean water level across the boundary (new addition that has not been pushed to Proteus yet, under test right now with encouraging results).

Also, using `cosh` and `sinh` instead of the fast version gives exactly the same results as the old version `WaveTools` for monochromatic waves. Closing.

@adimako response: 
  - **Velocity profile**: The velocity profile can be recovered for the whole water column by using `cosh` and `sinh` instead of `fastcosh` and `fastsinh` at the cost of computational power.
_This is only when for deep water waves, for intermediate and shallow water the fastcosh/fastsinh are a very good approximation for the profile_
  - **Pressure spikes**: Using `cos` gets rids of pressure spikes that could be encountered when the time step is fine due to approximations of `fastcos` ( @cekees @manuel-quezada )
_As already discussed, these spikes are due to discontinuities from the fastcos appoximation we noted that these spikes are dissipated outside of the relaxation zone._ 
  - **Water inflow**: Stokes drift velocity that caused the global water level to go up for nonlinear waves can be corrected by subtracting a relevant average velocity from the seabed to the mean water level across the boundary (new addition that has not been pushed to Proteus yet, under test right now with encouraging results).
_We confirmed that this works, although there are higher order stokes drifts that might cause inflow. @cekees I am wondering if there is an easy way to force the vof in the relaxation zone as we do for velocities, as this will ensure a steady level there. But for now I think this is acceptable_

comments.body: @tridelat - I'm actually looking at trying to do something similar in some in our discrete operators for the pressure convection diffusion problems so let's make sure to stay in communication about our progress on this.

I discussed this with Banks at USNCCM. I think I know how to do this now.  It's not really even a standard Robin condition. It ends up coupling all the pressure DOF on the solid boundary, and they do it by adding an additional equation.
@cekees is there literature about how they implemented it?

He didn't reference any literature on actual implementation details. You might be able to look in Overture. What he said was that they ADD an additional equation that sets basically uses the calculated body acceleration (from integrating the force around the boundary) to the fluid surface accelerations. issues.title: Replace all instances of `== None` with `is None`
issues.body:
To address https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/master/doc/release/1.13.0-notes.rst#futurewarning-to-changed-behavior , most instances of `==None` should be replaced with `is None`.
I believe that the current behavior of `==None` checks whether the object is simply `None`, but in the future `==None` will do an element wise comparison.  I think this means `[None, None, None] == None` would return `true` while `[None, None, None] is None` would return `false`.  I want to be sure this is what's happening, but if so I don't think there is any harm in changing `==None` to `is None`.

comments.body:
Good to point out the future behavior. The current hashstack `d3d27601f2de3c4538f11972f68973b142bdbc92` seems to be using a version of numpy that doesn't have the elementwise comparison implementation (version 1.12). 
```
>>> import numpy
>>> A = numpy.array([None,None,None])
>>> A == None
__main__:1: FutureWarning: comparison to `None` will result in an elementwise object comparison in the future.
False
>>> A[0] == None
True
```

If that's the case, then none of the current instances of `== None` should rely on this (future) elementwise comparison feature and would instead explicitly define a loop to do elementwise comparison. Long story short, I think we'll be okay in doing such a change; I'll try out the substitution in a new branch and see if Travis gives any issues.

I agree. My understanding is that the way we've been using it is equivalent to `is None` or `is not None` so a global replacement of these shouldn't change any behavior. I certainly can't think of any case where I've done anything using numpy arrays that would have elements that are None. If one of you two wants to take that on please go ahead. Thanks for looking into it.
Closing issue, now that #563 is merged in. Will reopen if similar issue arises in the future.

issues.title: use precise chrono compile flags for chrono extensions
issues.body:
I fixed the chrono extension builds with travis by explicitly adding '-mavx', but  we can do better than that.

We pull in information about hashdist packages from their build artifact using this script:
https://github.com/erdc-cm/proteus/blob/master/proteus/config/default.py#L38

We can extend this to pull in the chrono compilation options roughly as follows. 

1) get the installed ChronoConfig.cmake file:
```
CHRONO_INCLUDE_DIR, CHRONO_LIB_DIR = get_flags('chrono')
chrono_cmake_config_file = open(os.path.joint('CHRONO_LIB_DIR','cmake','ChronoConfig.cmake'),'r')
```
2) Parse that file to extract the string from the CHRONO_CXX_FLAGS line that looks something like this:

set(CHRONO_CXX_FLAGS " -std=c++14 -pthread -fopenmp  -march=native -msse4.2 -mfpmath=sse  -march=native -mavx2  -march=native -mfma")

3) Add those CHRONO_CXX_FLAGS to the mbd extensions in setup.py.

In an effort to be more systematic about our issues I'm assigning primary responsibility to @tridelat but Milad and I will help get this done before Milad leaves. @alistairbntl and @zhang-alvin it would be good to look at how similar things are done for petsc and scorec respectively.

issues.title: Systematic solver failure for 3D case on latest master
issues.body:
The latest master causes failures once per time step on the twp model (RANS2P) when running a 3D case, and this considerably increase the computational cost of running a simulation. It happens for a simple air/water 3D cuboidal domain with a still water level (free slip walls and atmophere BC on top).
I use the asm solver and run the case as follows:
`parun [case]_so.py -O [path to pets.options.asm`

It runs fine up to 5d5f1f5bb6e7934af33e7551749f11dd9e709186.
The next 2 commits, a052d8755c80549b7c0a3600cdfc52e7212706ee and 767d4e83ec6f1c34191ba08fdeb67fa0372ea701, the case does not run due to an error in `calculateJacobian()` of RANS2P (189 positional arguments given instead of 190).
From commit d99cf7539a717f67b9db446a938424261622fe33, it runs but gives me the failures at each time step. 

@cekees @alistairbntl @manuel-quezada , any idea what could cause this issue?

comments.body: I agree with @alistairbntl that this sounds like an inconsistency between the residual and the Jacobian on RANS2P. Do you have any 2D example in some repository or branch we can run?

These models: RANS2P and RANS3PF have the possibility of considering different terms to model different physics. In other words, we have the chance to add terms to the equations if we consider stuff like turbulence, Darcy's forces, particles (in the case of RANS3PF) and other things. In addition, we can consider different types of boundary conditions. All these "extra" terms are on top of the standard terms for the NS equations. First, we need to try to identify which of these terms is the one that is creating the problem (or the inconsistency between the residual and the Jacobian). I suggest we try to turn off everything that is not part of the standard form of the NS equations. If that works then we can start putting back these terms one by one.

@tridelat could you commit the case to a repository so we can try to reproduce the failure? I've tried the marin 3D test in conservative and nonconservative form, in parallel and serial, and with superlu and with asm. The Newton iteration is converging quadratically in all those cases. Maybe @alistairbntl and @manuel-quezada could try to reproduce the failure. Are you running on copper?

I was able to reproduce the problem on my linux machine and confirm that it runs with superlu in serial and superlu_dist in parallel, which would suggest the issue is in some of the recent linear algebra upgrades. The nonlinear residuals aren't decreasing as fast as I'd like even with a direct factorization. The first iteration shows the usual quadratic decrease but sometimes the second iteration doesn't produce a large decrease.

@cekees: It sounds like my errors on the `bug_asm` problem are different from yours.   (I'm on Proteus `master`: 867efbd, `hashstack`: fbf0d9 and air-water-vv `bug_asm`: cbb79ea).  Please let me know if you're experiencing something similar to the following:

When I run `bug_asm` using superlu_dist (two processors), I frequently get a residual increase during the first Navier-Stokes non-linear solve.  Because the solver is direct, the linear solve only takes a single step .  
At times (such as model substep t=6.51708e-01) the non-linear solver's behavior becomes more erratic (e.g. multiple residual increases and a large number of iterations before convergence.)  There are two points in the simulation at which the non-linear solver fails altogether. 
Towards the end of the simulation, the residual increase become less frequent, but they still pop up from time to time. 

When I run `bug_asm` with asm (two processors), the Navier Stokes I see similar things happen, but more frequently and dramatically.  For instance, the non-linear solver fails 10 times.   The linear solver also seems have trouble and 100+ gmres iterations are frequent.

Ultimately both simulations run to completion, and seem to generate the same solution profile in paraview.  The final solution looks as follows:

![solution_ex](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/10620679/31736130-e163a476-b411-11e7-8dff-ccd579bf134d.png)
I am confirming that the asm solver acts as intended on air-water-vv cbb79ea after the #628 merge, so this issue can be closed

The main dependencies we all know: petsc, hdf5, superlu, triangle, tetgen, but in some of the newer modules there are others like chrono, scipy, etc. I believe as long as you just comment out packages the stack rebuilds should go quickly and if you just remove proteus/linux2 the proteus modules won't rebuild either, so testing the stack by hand shouldn't take all that long and will shave some time off the downloads of the binaries. comments.body:
1. From a quick look at the listed packages, I don't see any exposure in the code to `julia` or `cgal`. The other packages that might not generally be used are packages for plotting like `openjpeg`, `matplotlib`, `matlab` and for manipulating certain data formats like GRIB ( `grib_api`). 

2. Some of the packages are needed in the C++ code (e.g. `scorec`), which would require more than just deleting `proteus/linux2` to reset the build. So unless it's too expensive, I'd rather just let Travis handle testing the stack profile. 

3. It might be useful to add a note next to each package indicating how they are used. That way, we can have a better idea of when packages become obsolete.

On 1) yes, and we can use `pip install` for matplotlib if it's not being used for any tests. On 2) hashdist is going to ensure that scorec dependencies are met, so unless there are undeclared dependencies in the scorec.yaml file deleting proteus/linux2 will regenerate the stack properly. hashdist uses a sort of build jail to  try to prevent linking to external dependencies accidentally. It's fine to let travis do the checking if you want to, but I was trying to save you time. Good idea on 3) about adding a note. You could just put a generic "optional package" in the ones you comment out for now.

1) It turns out matplotlib is used by the testing suite.
2) My concern was really that if a C++ extension/module was already compiled, the `.so` and `.a` files are not stored in `proteus/linux2` so even if I commented out some packages and deleted `proteus/linux2`, it wouldn't prompt a rebuild of the C++ libraries.

issues.title: Mass Correction: MCorr.postStep() behavior
issues.body:
I'm having some trouble understanding the mass correction procedure in terms of how the degrees of freedom are manipulated. In MCorr.postStep(), there are the following lines:
(https://github.com/erdc/proteus/blob/master/proteus/mprans/MCorr.py#L169-L173)
```
            self.lsModel.u[0].dof += self.massCorrModel.u[0].dof
            self.lsModel.q[('u', 0)] += self.massCorrModel.q[('u', 0)]
            self.lsModel.ebqe[('u', 0)] += self.massCorrModel.ebqe[('u', 0)]
            self.lsModel.q[('grad(u)', 0)] += self.massCorrModel.q[('grad(u)', 0)]
            self.lsModel.ebqe[('grad(u)', 0)] += self.massCorrModel.ebqe[('grad(u)', 0)]
```
This modifies the degrees of freedom and quadrature point fields of the level-set model, but this modification isn't reflected in the modelList.uList set of unknowns. So the result is the following sequence:

1.  MCorr.postStep() updates quadrature point fields and u.dof[:] of the level-set model
2.  RANS2P uses modified quadrature point fields
3.  Solver reaches level-set model again. When computing the residual, the modelList.uList set of unknowns writes over the u.dof[:] array.

This means that RANS2P uses the mass-corrected level-set field, but the level-set model is updating the uncorrected level-set field from the previous time step. 

Is this expected behavior or am I interpreting something wrong?

Example of behavior at step 3 in NCLS.getResidual(), just before calling `self.setUnknowns()` at https://github.com/erdc/proteus/blob/master/proteus/mprans/NCLS.py#L1185:

```
(Pdb) print self.u[0].dof.mean()
0.0754403492887
(Pdb) print u.mean()
0.0754478228232
```
 and just after the call

```
(Pdb) print self.u[0].dof.mean()
0.0754478228232
(Pdb) print u.mean()
0.0754478228232
```

comments.body:
There's also a difference between VOF.uList[:] and VOF.levelModelList[0].u.dof[:] as well because of the call to setMassQuadrature() in postStep():
https://github.com/zhang-alvin/proteus/blob/master/proteus/mprans/MCorr.py#L1140.

@zhang-alvin Here are several remarks on your concern
1.  Yes. `.uList` is different from `.u.dof`.  They have different structure and `xxx.u.dof` has the additional information of Dirichlet boundary condition.
2.  The 3 execution sequence you said is correct for me. But, it does not mean that the uncorrected value is used in the next step because the reference is used https://github.com/erdc/proteus/blob/05d9d7bf0912f7e1831ca04f149a803ab605e2d6/proteus/mprans/NCLS.py#L703
3. In each time step, several Newton iteration steps are needed. So that is why in `xxx.setUnknowns` of `xxx.getResidual` the variable `xxx.u.dof` is assigend to be `u` before computing the residual (of `u`).

@wacyyang I can understand points 1. and 3. I don't think 2. addresses my concern though. To clarify my concern, if I'm solving for time `t_(n+1)`, I'm observing that I have two different level set fields from time t_n, `phi` and `phi_corrected` and these are stored in the `.uList` and `.u.dof` structures, respectively. 

a) RANS2P uses the quadrature values from `phi_corrected`
b) LS calls `setUnknowns`, which moves the `.uList` (which is `phi) values to `.u.dof`.  
`self.q[('u',0)]` is computed within `calculateResidual()` based on the nodal fields, which is now `phi` and not `phi_corrected`.

A follow-up question: shouldn't the values in `.uList` and `.u.dof` for a model be equivalent after completing the solve at a given time step?

@zhang-alvin In you example, can you print out the location of the different values in `phi` and `phi_correct`? I think the difference is on the Dirichlet boundary. For your question, I think they are the same (except Dirichlet boundary information) when Newton Solver finishes. But, they may become different after `postStep`.

@wacyyang If I compare the two structures: `print u==self.u[0].dof` in `getResidual()` before `setUnknowns`, I have that all values are `False` which is to say that no values are the same between `phi` and `phi_correct`. 

I don't see why we want them to become different after `postStep`.

After a discussion with @wacyyang, most of my confusion is resolved. The heart of the issue is the choice in initial guess for the level-set model. It shouldn't be a problem that uList or `phi` is used as an initial guess instead of `phi_corrected` because the initial guess can be "anything". 

My next question is why is `phi_corrected` not used instead as the initial guess?

@zhang-alvin and @wacyyang thanks for looking at this. The uList storage is manipulated following NumericalSolution.pre/postStep after the models' pre/postStep based on what is provided in the copyInstructions: https://github.com/erdc/proteus/blob/master/proteus/NumericalSolution.py#L1648. I'll let you work through the logic on your own, but the basic idea is to provide some instructions to either a) set the uList values to zero b) copy the uList values from some other model, or c) reset the uList from the models own internal DOF.  

It's true that the uList storage is essentially the initial guess to the nonlinear iteration so the results should be independent of it for tight tolerances (and convergent nonlinear iterations). Specifically for  NCLS and VOF, which are linear models anyway, it's unlikely to have an effect and would trigger an extra residual call.  Likewise MCORR should be reset to zero anyway. RDLS could be sensitive to the initial guess though. You're welcome to play around with the copyInstructions on your branch to see if you get better results.

@cekees Thanks for the explanation. Resetting the uList models will make information transfer simpler when using MeshAdapt and the code much cleaner.

`postStep()` also operates on the boundary quadrature for the gradient of the level-set:

```self.lsModel.ebqe[('grad(u)', 0)] += self.massCorrModel.ebqe[('grad(u)', 0)]```
in https://github.com/erdc/proteus/blob/master/proteus/mprans/MCorr.py#L173

but I don't see where the `ebqe[('grad(u)',0)]` vector is populated on each time step or reset. Instead, I'm seeing that the `MCorr.postStep()` is the only time `ebqe[('grad(u)',0]` is modified, which leads to a continuous history of the values from the beginning of the simulation, which doesn't seem right. And this data structure is used somewhere because modifying this behavior changes the pressure gauge results for my test case. Where is this structure used and is this the expected behavior?

`self.massCorrModel.ebqe[('grad(u)',0)]` structure is populated by 
```ebqe_n[ebNE_kb_nSpace+I] = grad_u_ext[I]/norm;``` 
in `https://github.com/erdc/proteus/blob/master/proteus/mprans/MCorr.h#L890

The self.lsModel.ebqe[('grad(u)', 0)]  for a signed distance field is also the unit normal of the level set (n_ls), which is used in various places in the level set methodology and set/calculated in in NCLS and RDLS.  When we correct the level set we also correct the gradient as we're doing here, which is consistent with the definition of the level set correction. That is, self.massCorrModel.ebqe[('grad(u)',0)] is the correction to the gradient of the level set. The renormalizing of the gradient correction is questionable, but I don't think it relates to your problems with MeshAdapt.

As I said, you can play around with the copyInstructions on your branch, but I don't think you need to be modifying this code to fix your issues with meshAdapt. If you need to reset information at the various quadrature point sets after adaptivity, then do it by calling the proper functions, as is done in postStep and preStep in NumericalSolution and/or by evaluation residuals after adaptivity.

issues.title: Redistancing: RD.postStep() behavior
issues.body:
Similar to #766 but for redistancing.

https://github.com/erdc/proteus/blob/master/proteus/mprans/RDLS.py#L280-L282

```
                self.nModel.u[0].dof.flat[:] = self.rdModel.u[0].dof.flat[:]
                self.nModel.calculateCoefficients()
                self.nModel.calculateElementResidual()
```
where nModel is the level-set model.
The LS.u.dof[:] data structure is modified and the quadrature point fields are updated in the call to `calculateElementResidual()`. The redistanced quadrature point fields are fed into RANS2P, but what is updated in the level-set model in the next time step is the non-redistanced field from LS.uList. 

My understanding is that the uList is effectively the solution that we care about and that is what is updated when solving a particular model. 

Again, is this expected behavior or a misinterpretation?

issues.title: RANS2P LES, non-conservative form, dynamic viscosity not updated?
issues.body:
In `evaluateCoefficients()` in `RANS2P.h`, the eddy-viscosity is computed for the classic and dynamic Smagorinsky models. The total kinematic viscosity is updated to include the eddy-viscosity:
https://github.com/erdc/proteus/blob/master/proteus/mprans/RANS2P.h#L671 ,
and for the conservative form, this total kinematic viscosity is used in the "diffusion tensor"
https://github.com/erdc/proteus/blob/master/proteus/mprans/RANS2P.h#L918-L943

But for the non-conservative form, the "diffusion tensor" depends on the dynamic viscosity, but it is **not** updated with the `eddy-viscosity x rho`: 
https://github.com/erdc/proteus/blob/master/proteus/mprans/RANS2P.h#L672

The only other time `eddy_viscosity` is used is in the `updateTurbulenceClosure()` function: https://github.com/erdc/proteus/blob/master/proteus/mprans/RANS2P.h#L1142
But `updateTurbulenceClosure()` is not called for classical or dynamic Smagorinsky.

issues.title: Unify VOF, VOF3P and VOS3P
issues.body:
This issue is to incorporate a recently implemented solver for the linear conservation law under non divergence free velocity fields. The idea is to apply subsequent FCT steps to impose global bounds based on a max saturated concentration. The first FCT is global and uses a discrete upwinded solution as target and the old solution as safeguard goal when the global upper bound is violated. Note that the target solution is positivity preserving and moreover MPP (thanks to discrete upwinding) but it doesn't satisfy the global upper bound. Afterwards, we consider a high-order discretization of the transport equation and apply standard Zalesak's FCT. The code is in VOF.h within `mquezada/VOS`. We want to: 

- Clean up the code. 
- Compare and discuss about unifying `VOF`, `VOF3P` and `VOS3P`.
- Test the unified implementation specially for saturated flows.

comments.body: @cekees - Quick question.  The functions declared in `proteus_lapack.h` have the pure LAPACK handles (e.g. `dgetrf_` etc).  In contrast, the function wrappers declared in `lapackWrappersModule.c` (no corresponding `.h` file btw, so I'm guessing these functions are not forward declared anywhere) have names like `denseFactorPrepare` / `lapackWrappersDenseFactorPrepare`.  Am I correct to assume that my `clapack.pyx` file should actually be forward declaring these functions, not the LAPACK handles?

You want to declare what you will use from proteus_lapack.h and proteus_blas.h and then you want to define the classes and functions that are defined in lapackWrappersModule.c.  This a little more advanced than just wrapping functions because lapackWrappersModule actually defines a new  Python class (type) called DenseFactor and some functions that operate on that new type (lapackWrappersDenseFactorPrepare, etc.).  See http://docs.cython.org/en/latest/src/tutorial/cdef_classes.html

Another way to look  at is how the lapackWrappers modules is  used:

Creating a DenseFactor object:
```
self.denseFactor = lapackWrappers.DenseFactor(self.n)
```
Preparing  (factoring) the object:
```
lapackWrappers.denseFactorPrepare(self.n,
                                              self.L,
                                              self.denseFactor)
```
Solving a system with the prepared (factored) object:
```
lapackWrappers.denseFactorSolve(self.n,
                                            self.L,
                                            self.denseFactor,
                                            u)
```

Calculating the eigenvalue with the object:

```
            lapackWrappers.denseCalculateEigenvalues(self.JOBVL,
                                                     self.JOBVR,
                                                     self.n,
                                                     self.Leig,
                                                     self.n,
                                                     self.eigenvalues_r,
                                                     self.eigenvalues_i,
                                                     self.leftEigenvectors,
                                                     self.n,
                                                     self.rightEigenvectors,
                                                     self.n,
                                                     self.work,
                                                     5*self.n)```

No problem. Good to know the story behind it. The archiving needs a good cleaning soon, so I'd be interested it any performance information. We could probably add some options to selectively disable archiving for some fields.

@tridelat and @manuel-quezada  here is a simple example of object-based physics and numerics in a single-file problem description: https://github.com/erdc/proteus/blob/master/proteus/tests/periodic/duct.py

The basic idea is to just walk through the needed models setting up a default object and then overriding the options, then set up the global system parameters. e.g. 
```
from proteus.defaults import (Physics_base, Numerics_base)
# Navier-Stokes physics
nse_p = Physics_base()
nse_p.LevelModel = RANS3PF.LevelModel.
...
# Navier-Stokes numerics
nse_n = Numerics_base()
nse_n =  LinearSolver.KSP_Petsc4py
...
# CLSVOF physics
clsvof_p = Physics_base()
...
# CLSVOF_numerics
clsvof_n = Numerics_base()
...
# global system
from proteus.default_so import *
pnList=[(nse_p, nse_n),
             (clsvof_p, clsvof_n)]
...
```
This avoids the necessity of doing `from proteus.default_p import *`, etc. and the dangers that involves due to the fact that Python modules are singleton. I would like to get rid of that last `from proteus.default_so import *`, but I have thought through the best way to do that yet. We could just have parun check for the existence of a single `so` object that could be initialized in the same manner.

It's not clear to me what the goal for `TwoPhaseFlow` is. With it's current capabilities, it looks like it's the interface which most users should be building cases in Proteus since it can handle domain generation, mesh generation, and analysis specification in a single file. 

The initialization function of `TwoPhaseFlowProblem` assumes that the user is using some combination of a flow model and interface tracking models. Should it be allowed to handle single phase problems or should that be some other app like `OnePhaseFlowProblem`? As of now, it isn't very clean in terms of adding additional models like body dynamics. 

For example, in the 2D floating body example, there's a need to specify the indices of the models:
https://github.com/erdc/proteus_tutorial/blob/master/2d/floating2D_chrono.py#L228-L233

In the dambreak case, there's no need to specify those indices because they're automatically defined via `TwoPhaseFlow`:
https://github.com/erdc/proteus_tutorial/blob/master/2d/dambreak.py

On a separate note, I think the initialization function can be condensed from

```
def __init__(self,
                 ns_model=0, #0: rans2p, 1: rans3p
                 ls_model=1, #0: vof+ncls+rdls+mcorr, 1: clsvof
                 nd=2,
                 # TIME STEPPING #
                 cfl=0.33,
                 outputStepping=None,
                 # DOMAIN AND MESH #
                 structured=False,
                 he=None,
                 nnx=None,
                 nny=None,
                 nnz=None,
                 domain=None,
                 triangleFlag=0,
                 # INITIAL CONDITIONS #
                 initialConditions=None,
                 # BOUNDARY CONDITIONS #
                 boundaryConditions=None,
                 # AUXILIARY VARIABLES #
                 auxVariables=None,
                 # OTHERS #
                 useSuperlu=True,
                 fastArchive=False)
```

to 

```
def __init__(self, 
                   domain = domain,
                   models = modelList,
                   other = otherOptions)
```

The boundary and initial conditions need to be attached to their respective models within Proteus anyway, so it's better to just have the user be directly responsible for adding it in after the `TwoPhaseFlowProblem` instantiation. Several of the other flags such as `nd` and `he` can be attributes of the `domain` object. 

The `modelList` could be a user-defined list of model objects that defines the ordering of the staggered solve and allows users to easily incorporate body dynamics or any other model. To avoid new-user confusion, we could define a `default_modelList = [rans2p_model,vof_model,ls_model,rd_model,mc_model]`.

My understanding is that  https://github.com/erdc/proteus/blob/master/proteus/TwoPhaseFlow/utils/petsc.options.asm is not a needed file anymore because of 

https://github.com/erdc/proteus/blob/master/proteus/TwoPhaseFlow/utils/Parameters.py#L1483

from PR #954

issues.title: Automatic documentation build
issues.body:
So right now, the "new" documentation is on a separate repository (proteus-doc), and the process to push documentation is not automatic at all. There are 3 ways to do it:
- Manual: build the intended version of proteus; build doc locally to specific folder; add changed files, new files, and remove unused files; commit; push to gh-pages branch.
- readthedocs: can automatically document Proteus, fully externally. Ideal, but would require an install of Proteus for it to work properly, and readthedocs build time limit is around 900s, and I don't think there is a way to point at an existing build (not 100% sure about that).
- Travis: can automatically build doc and push it to `gh-pages`, but only when someone commits to specific branch (such as master).

The last 2 require the **documentation to be in the main repository** (proteus), and there is a way to bring changes to the documentation from proteus-doc to proteus without loosing commit authorship. I think the Travis solution might be the best one where a full installation of Proteus can be used for sphinx. This will make it very easy for anyone to add a page to the documentation and have it built as soon as it is committed to master.
The only issue I can see with that technique is that Travis could potentially time out when committing to master while it didn't on a PR because now it would also need to build the documentation.
Should we go that route?
@cekees

It basically just downloads `xtensor-python` and its dependencies, and adds their include directories when compiling xtensor-based extensions.

Yes, I don't think there is already a base recipe for a header-only package, but you can so something like the autotools recipe without the `make` stage and simply copying the headers to the $ARTIFACT/include directory:

https://github.com/erdc/hashstack/blob/master/base/autotools_package.yaml

The distutils package package install command just explicitly installs into $ARTIFACT as the prefix, so maybe that's a better example:

https://github.com/erdc/hashstack/blob/master/base/distutils_package.yaml
`xtensor` is now integrated in the hdist build.

issues.title: TPF: __init__ functions for models has unnecessary logic
issues.body:
Based on discussions with @tridelat 

In the initialization of some models' coefficients class, like `RANS2P.Coefficients`, there is 
already logical evaluations based on the model attributes:

https://github.com/erdc/proteus/blob/master/proteus/mprans/RANS2P.py#L238-L275

This means that the class cannot be instantiated without appropriate attributes being set. This makes the code harder to read and is less user-friendly than necessary.

The proposal is to move such logical statements under a new function, e.g. `RANS2P.Coefficients.start()` after the user has specified the desired attributes. This has the added bonus of eliminating the need for the `CoefficientsOptions` class.

Such a change can be applied to all models.

comments.body: Closing as this was addressed with #1070

issues.title: TPF: proposal for refactoring initial conditions
issues.body:
The current method to set initial conditions is through a user-specified dictionary

```
theProblem.modelDict['flow'].p.initialConditions={0: zero(),
                            1: zero(),
                            2: zero()}
theProblem.modelDict['vof'].p.initialConditions={0: VF_IC()}
theProblem.modelDict['ls'].p.initialConditions={0: PHI_IC()}
theProblem.modelDict['rd'].p.initialConditions={0: PHI_IC()}
```
The user has to know that for the `rans2p` or `rans3p` models, 0 corresponds to pressure. The use of numerical keys for the dictionary doubles as indices when setting the `numpy arrays` for the dofs in https://github.com/erdc/proteus/blob/master/proteus/Transport.py#L1627-L1650.

To make this more user friendly, we can ...
1. force the user to use specific keywords as keys
```
theProblem.modelDict['flow'].p.initialConditions={"pressure": zero(),
                            "u": zero(),
                            "v": zero()}
```
We can then keep a separate dictionary to map the keywords to indices to use the current approach to set the `numpy` arrays
```
idxDict = {"pressure": 0, "u": 1, "v": 2} 
```

2. Alternatively, we can define an `InitialCondition` class for each model which forces the user to populate specific attributes:

```
        class InitialCondition(FreezableClass):
            def __init__(self):
                self.pressure = None
                self.u = None
                self.v = None
                self.w= None
       

        self.p.initialConditions = InitialCondition()
        ...
        self.p.initialConditions._freeze()
```
user would set pressure condition as follows:
```
theProblem.modelDict['flow'].p.initialConditions.pressure=zero()
```
We can then use the internal class dictionary (e.g. `self.p.initialConditions.__dict__["pressure"]`) along with an index dictionary as with the first approach to populate the `numpy` arrays. The advantage with the second approach is that the freezing capability prevents the user from adding/defining attributes and throws an error very quickly.

issues.title: Migrating mprans to xtensor
issues.body:
This issue is meant to track the migration of the mprans module to `xtensor`. This will be splitted in many steps to ease the merge of PRs and avoid having too many conflicts.

- [x] Replace C-style arrays with `pyarray` in the C++ api exposed to Python
- [x] Replace all the arguments with a dictionnary of arguments
- [ ] Move implementations to cpp files
- [ ] Propagate `pyarray` to the implementation
- [ ] Simplify the implementation based on `xtensor` API.

Having finished the repo cleanup, I'm concerned if large files are ever added into the repository again. I haven't found a GitHub app that can check/compare added file sizes for PRs, so a partial solution is to add a PR template to remind developers and reviewers to check such things. 

There might be other things we can add to the template (e.g. don't use import *, suggest naming schemes for variables).

issues.title: PointGauges variables with underscore text parsing
issues.body:
If a model has variables such as `['h', 'h_u', 'h_v']`, the following piece of code will not work: 

heightPointGauges = PointGauges(gauges=((('h_u'), ((7.56, 16.05,  0),
                                                 (7.56, 14.55, 0),
                                                 (7.56, 13.05, 0),
                                                 (7.56, 11.55, 0),
                                                 (9.36, 13.80, 0),
                                                 (10.36, 13.80, 0),
                                                 (12.96, 11.22, 0),
                                                 (15.56, 13.80, 0))),),
                                activeTime=(0., opts.final_time),
                                fileName='island_wave_gauges.csv')
but 

heightPointGauges = PointGauges(gauges=((('h'), ((7.56, 16.05,  0),
                                                 (7.56, 14.55, 0),
                                                 (7.56, 13.05, 0),
                                                 (7.56, 11.55, 0),
                                                 (9.36, 13.80, 0),
                                                 (10.36, 13.80, 0),
                                                 (12.96, 11.22, 0),
                                                 (15.56, 13.80, 0))),),
                                activeTime=(0., opts.final_time),
                                fileName='island_wave_gauges.csv')
will work. The loop line seen here https://github.com/erdc/proteus/blob/master/proteus/Gauges.py#L67 separates the `h_u` variable into three separate characters. A hack involves surrounding the single variable with `[]` as follows: `(['h_u'])`. However, surrounding multiple single variables like `(['h'],['h_u'])` gives an error.

comments.body: @zhang-alvin

@ejtovar what about `('h_u',)` and `('h', 'h_u')`, or `['h_u']` and `['h', 'h_u']`?
I think your problem here is that putting parentheses around a string without a comma does not make it a tuple (`('h_u')` is equivalent to just `'h_u'`), so your code worked fine only if your unique string had a single character. Parentheses are also superfluous for `(['h_u'])`, this works because it is a list
Yes, you are correct!
Perhaps we should add a conditional to where the fields are parsed to check if the argument is a tuple and if not, make it a tuple. It seems bizarre for the user to know this.

> Perhaps we should add a conditional to where the fields are parsed to check if the argument is a tuple and if not, make it a tuple. It seems bizarre for the user to know this.

@zhang-alvin There are many places in the code where we are supposed to pass a list of variables even if there is only one variable for some cases in practice.
An extra conditional would not hurt if that makes things easier, but making non-tuple arguments become tuples could cause issues (what if the user passes a list of strings?). Checking if it is a string (field variables are strings here), and if it is, making it a list or a tuple would work better though.

Anyway, I think the confusion came from the use of tuples within tuples when calling `PointGauges` here, but those can be replaced by lists instead for clarity. Also, the documentation does mention that it must be a "set of fields to be monitored":
https://proteustoolkit.org/api/proteus.Gauges.html (there is even an example with a single field variable `('p',)`)
If it is confusing, it might be worth updating the documentation, but don't forget to "read (and update) the docs"™ ;)

issues.title: automate zoltan partitioning and genPUMI stage
issues.body: When we run with the PUMI workflow for existing domain/mesh types, we need to run an unmodified input file to generate the mesh and let PUMI build its own representation of the domain geometry. Then we need to run zsplit to partition it and run a different input file to run in adaptivity. issues.title: Updating arrays after MoveMesh step
issues.body:
There are a number of data structures that are not properly updated after a MoveMesh step. 

`postStep()` (https://github.com/erdc/proteus/blob/master/proteus/mprans/MoveMesh.py#L123) updates the `mesh.nodeArray` which stores the coordinates of the vertices. 

There is also a separate `updateAfterMeshMotion` function (https://github.com/erdc/proteus/blob/master/proteus/mprans/MoveMesh.py#L801) that is called before the next MoveMesh step, which seems to update the element and boundary quadrature fields. 

Neither update the `nodeDiametersArray` or `elementDiametersArray` used in the computation of the Heaviside function. 

Neither update the coefficient weighting in the point gauges, which would lead to inaccurate point gauge readings when the mesh is moved. Similar issues should arise when identifying segments for the line gauges. 

Updating the node diameters is simple with a call to `cmeshTools.computeGeometricInfo`. Updating the gauges might wind up to be quite expensive (e.g. what if a point gauge now lies on a different element because of the mesh motion). 

I'm putting this issue up to get some ideas, maybe have a discussion. I think that all these updates should occur during postStep of the MoveMesh model with the ability to influence the data structures/arrays in other models if necessary. There may also be a way to smartly update the structures used to obtain the local mesh entities of interest (e.g. k-d tree).

issues.title: hpc job templates in config
issues.body:
Many of the hpc machines have required local config changes, which we include in proteus/config/MACHINE.py. While the require changes are becoming less invasive, we are running into more users who have trouble submitting jobs and running tests on hpc machines. I think we could write into our machine configs both the MPI launch script (mpiexec, aprun, mpiexec_mpt, etc.) and a template job submission script (e.g. a PBS script template suitable for the machine). With that information, I think we could support something like this from the login node:

`hpc_machine> parun myproblem.py` 

This would automatically submit an interactive batch job to the debug queue for 1 hour and run the given parun command with the required MPI launcher on 1 core (or n cores with a parun -n option)
 
`parun myproblem.py -Q "-A ERDCV00898R40 -q standard -l walltime=001:00:00"`

This would run the command in a batch job (or interactive job if -I is included).

issues.title: CNW with CombineWaves, RandomWaves, NewWave
issues.body:
Hi, I'm looking to create a CNW (Time Domain Simulation of Jack-up Dynamics With the Extremes of a Gaussian Process, Taylor et al 1997) eta time series

I'm trying to generate it using the `wavetools` module, but I'm unsure about certain steps to create the involved classes.

First, I'm trying to create the `NewWave` object.
I had previously implmented this myself, approaching the problem by assuming very large water depth, unidirectional waves, etc
After reading through the `NewWave` class help and looking at the source code, I'm having a bit of trouble generating the `NewWave `object using these simplifications
How would I approach this?
I assume that I can pass a 1-element array to both the `waveDir` and `g` arguments to only consider a single wave direction, but is there any way of considering water depth large (so tanh(kd) ≈ 1)?  Does inputting a sufficiently large depth parameter (i.e., ~500m) work?

Additionally, I'm unsure what the `mwl` argument is used for, or how is it defined. I assume it's a parameter used to calculate the velocity of wave particles, but I'm not interested in that output. Is it possible to not input such argument (or inputting a "garbage" without it affecting the eta time series)?

These doubts apply to the `RandomWaves` class too (`mwl`, `depth`, `waveDir` and `g`)

Finally, regarding the generation of a CNW, would the `CombineWave` class be a suitable match?
The docs and source code provide little insight on the inner workings of the class

comments.body:
hello @ghylander. Few points to help you:

- mwl is the level of the water according to coordinates, e.g. if your gravity direction is aligned with the z axis and the water level is set at z=10 - then mwl = 10
- depth is the distance from the seabed (assuming a flat seabed) e.g if the seabed is at z=-10 then according to previous example, depth=20
- waveDir is the unit vector aligned with direction of the wave according to the global coordinate system, e.g if your waves run along the x axis then waveDir = [1,0.,0.]
- g is the gravity acceleration vector e.g. for the previous example g=[0,0,-9.81]. This means that the gravity is aligned with the z axis and pointing downwards (toward negative values)
- For deep water waves assume that the depth is >0.5 x wavelenght. The wavelength in deep water is depth = 1.56 T^2 where T is the period

Hi @adimako, thanks for your comment.

The first two points (regarding `mwl` and `depth`) were very insightful. I didn't understand the difference between the two. Now I understand the former is the distance between the z=0 origin and the water surface point and the letter the actual distance between the surface and the seabed.

Thanks for the comments on how to input the `waveDir` and `g` parameters, I had the wrong idea about how to input them.

Thanks for your comments! I was able to succesfully create the objects and execute the `eta` and `writeEtaSeries` methods.

~~I also have found that the wavetools.NewWave.writeEtaSeries() method does not write the results to file (as it seems it should do)~~ Nevermind, there was a permission error exception being silently caught


Finally, my question regarding the suitability of the `CombineWaves` class to create a Constrained NewWave eta tiemseries from the `NewWave` and `RandomWaves` objects does remain.

The `CombineWaves` class assumes the principle of superposition applies to solutions. That is, it sums wave heights (or velocities) over the list of wave objects ("wave conditions") provided by the user: https://github.com/erdc/proteus/blob/main/proteus/WaveTools.py#L3328.

I see thanks

Would you be interested in a CNW theory implementation for proteus?
I can provide the basic python code, but I don't have experience with cython to the point where I could fully implement it

Yes, probably the thing to do is get things implemented in WaveTools.py first, along with tests covering the new class added to https://github.com/erdc/proteus/blob/main/proteus/tests/wave_tests/test_wavetools.py.  The process is basically to fork proteus and then do a pull request from your fork with your changes. The general requirements for accepting a PR are that it provides something useful and does not decrease test coverage. We can worry about optimizing it via Cython or pybind once the pure Python PR is ready to merge. @adimako may have more comments on what constitutes useful functionality for the WaveTools module--he is the main author of that. If you wanted to continue with the PR, you can close this issue. We can discuss further once you have an initial PR.

Some notes before I get to work and opening a PR

How would you like the class to be used?
To apply the theory, first one would create a random wave, with its own Hs, Tp, etc
Then, the NewWave is generated (using the appropriate Hs, Tp, etc). The NewWave formula is not applied, however. Only the auto-correlation function (or unit NewWave) is needed. 
The required parameters for the CNW are the following:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/74593034/195786946-5a252a31-8453-48b2-8755-4920bc2ad165.png)
(image source: Non-Linear Analysis of Jack-Up Structures Subjected to Random Waves, M. Cassidy 1999)

 (1) The random waves surface elevation time series η<sub>rw</sub>(t)
 (2) The unit NewWave r(t)
 (3) The NewWave scaling factor (α, A<sub>cr</sub> or `wt.NewWave()` 'Hs' parameter)
 (4) The random waves surface elevation at t=t<sub>f</sub> or `wt.NewWave()` 'tfocus' parameter)
 (5) The unit NewWave slope ṙ(t)
 (5*) λ<sup>2</sup>, extracted from the 2<sup>nd</sup> spectral moment of the wave energy spectrum (m<sub>2</sub>=λ<sup>2</sup>·σ<sup>2</sup>)
 (6) The constrained surface slope ἁ (for a crest, ἁ=0)
 (7) The random waves surface elevation at t=t<sub>f</sub>

And the auto-correlation function or unit NewWave (r(t) or ρ(t)) is defined as (A new model for the kinematics of large ocean waves-application as a design wave, Tromans 1991):
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/74593034/195789753-5590a8c6-3819-4389-b220-e1f96a127611.png)
Where τ= t - t<sub>f</sub>,

Given all of this, how would you like the class to be constructed?
Do you want to generate a RandomWaves object and pass it to the ConstrainedNewWave class?
Do you want the random waves to be generated fully inside the ConstrainedNewWave class?
How do you want to define at what point in time inside the random waves eta series the NewWave is constrained? (In the equation above, t=0 is defined as t<sub>f</sub>)

Any option is good for me, but how do you want the object to be constructed by the user?

issues.title: config/default.py: SUPERLU paths bypass get_flags(), plus two duplicated assignments
issues.body:
Three small defects in `proteus/config/default.py`, all present on `main` at `e52b5ad3`. None breaks the default conda/pip build; they surface when proteus is built against externally-provided packages (spack, or any `<PKG>_DIR` workflow).

## 1. `SUPERLU_DIR` is never honoured

`default.py:298-300`:

```python
PROTEUS_SUPERLU_INCLUDE_DIR = PROTEUS_PETSC_INCLUDE_DIR
PROTEUS_SUPERLU_LIB_DIR = pjoin(prefix, 'lib64')
PROTEUS_SUPERLU_LIB_DIR = pjoin(prefix, 'lib')
```

where `prefix` is `PROTEUS_PREFIX` or `sys.exec_prefix` (`default.py:8-10`).

The file already has a helper for exactly this, and its docstring states the intent:

```python
package_dir_env = os.getenv(package.upper() + '_DIR')   # default.py:65
```

> "This supports building Proteus using packages provides via environment variables."

`proteus/config/thunder.py:23` uses it:

```python
PROTEUS_SUPERLU_INCLUDE_DIR, PROTEUS_SUPERLU_LIB_DIR = get_flags('superlu')
```

`default.py` does not, so setting `SUPERLU_DIR` has no effect there.

Line 298 is correct for exactly one layout: a PETSc configured with `--download-superlu`, which does install `slu_ddefs.h` into its own include dir. That is the most common way proteus is built, which is presumably why this has gone unnoticed. It is not what the other two layouts do:

- **conda:** `slu_ddefs.h` is owned by the separate `superlu` package, not by `petsc`. I checked eight proteus envs here and it is `superlu-*.json` in every one. It resolves only because conda's single prefix means `PROTEUS_PETSC_INCLUDE_DIR` and superlu's headers are the same directory.
- **spack:** `petsc+superlu` links spack's own superlu package and does *not* vendor the headers. `petsc-3.25.4-*/include/slu_ddefs.h` is absent; `superlu-7.0.1-*/include/slu_ddefs.h` is present. The build succeeds only because spack's compiler wrapper injects superlu's `-I`/`-L` implicitly for a direct dependency — no `-I...superlu` appears in the build log, yet `SuperLU_timer_` ends up linked into `superluWrappers*.so`.

So the header is found by accident of layout in two of the three cases, and a build system that provides superlu at its own prefix has no supported way to say so. Proteus has long supported both an externally built superlu and a PETSc-downloaded one; only the latter currently works through `default.py`.

Reported downstream in the spack packaging review: https://github.com/spack/spack-packages/pull/6000

**Suggested fix:** use `get_flags('superlu')` in `default.py` as `thunder.py` does, falling back to the current PETSc-include behaviour when `SUPERLU_DIR` is unset. That keeps the `--download-superlu` path working unchanged while making an externally built superlu addressable.

## 2. `PROTEUS_SUPERLU_LIB_DIR` is assigned twice

Lines 299 and 300 above. The `lib64` assignment is immediately overwritten by `lib` and is dead. Presumably one was meant to be conditional on the platform.

## 3. `-DPROTEUS_USE_SIMMETRIX` is appended twice

`default.py:294` and `:296`, both at indent 2 inside the same `if os.getenv('SIM_INCLUDE_DIR') is not None:` block:

```python
  PROTEUS_SCOREC_EXTRA_COMPILE_ARGS = PROTEUS_SCOREC_EXTRA_COMPILE_ARGS + ['-DPROTEUS_USE_SIMMETRIX']

  PROTEUS_SCOREC_EXTRA_COMPILE_ARGS = PROTEUS_SCOREC_EXTRA_COMPILE_ARGS + ['-DPROTEUS_USE_SIMMETRIX']
```

Defining the macro twice on the command line is harmless, so this is cosmetic — but it looks like a bad merge and the duplicate should go.

## Notes

All three found while reviewing how the spack `py-proteus` package passes dependency prefixes; (1) is the one with practical consequences. Happy to open a PR for any or all of these.

issues.title: config/default.py: detect cray-libsci instead of guessing OpenBLAS
issues.body:
## Problem

`proteus/config/default.py` assumes OpenBLAS when PETSc does not report a
BLAS/LAPACK library:

```python
PROTEUS_BLAS_LIB   = 'openblas'
PROTEUS_LAPACK_LIB = 'openblas'
```

On a Cray EX system there is no OpenBLAS. BLAS and LAPACK come from
**cray-libsci**, so the link fails outright and takes the whole wheel build
down:

```
ld: cannot find -lopenblas: No such file or directory
```

`get_petsc_blaslapack()` cannot rescue this. It parses `BLASLAPACK_LIB` out of
PETSc's `petscvariables`, and on a Cray that variable is **empty** — PETSc is
configured with `--with-blaslapack` and picks libsci up implicitly through the
`cc`/`CC` compiler wrappers, so it has no library name to record. The helper
correctly returns `None` and we fall through to the OpenBLAS guess.

The result is that **every Cray EX machine needs a hand-written config file**
that exists only to say "BLAS is libsci". Of the four HPCMP machines on our ARO
allocation, three had no config at all and failed exactly this way; the fourth,
Carpenter, had one but hardcoded `sci_cray`, which only exists under
PrgEnv-cray. See cekees/proteus#26 and #28, which add
`carpenter.py`/`barfoot.py`/`blueback.py`/`narwhal.py` for 1.9.1.

Those four files are nearly identical and carry no machine-specific knowledge —
they are all `from .carpenter import *` plus a dispatch entry. That is a strong
signal the logic belongs in `default.py`.

## Proposal for 2.0

Detect cray-libsci in `default.py` rather than requiring a file per machine.
The information is already in the environment:

- `$CRAY_LIBSCI_PREFIX_DIR` is set by the `cray-libsci` module and points at
  the libsci tree for the **currently loaded** Programming Environment.
- The flavour follows the PrgEnv: `libsci_cray*` under PrgEnv-cray,
  `libsci_gnu*` under PrgEnv-gnu. Hardcoding either breaks the other.

Roughly what the per-machine configs do today, hoisted into the Linux branch of
`default.py` ahead of the OpenBLAS fallback:

```python
_libsci_dir = os.path.join(os.getenv("CRAY_LIBSCI_PREFIX_DIR", ""), "lib")
if glob.glob(os.path.join(_libsci_dir, "libsci_cray.*")):
    _libsci = "sci_cray"
elif glob.glob(os.path.join(_libsci_dir, "libsci_gnu.*")):
    _libsci = "sci_gnu"
```

Two details worth preserving from the 1.9.1 work:

- **Detect, do not assume.** Carpenter's config only ever worked under
  PrgEnv-cray, while proteus is verified on GCC 11.4/13.3/15.2 and has never
  been verified on Cray clang.
- **Match the plain name, not an ABI-suffixed one.** Older libsci trees carry
  both `libsci_gnu.so` and e.g. `libsci_gnu_82.so` (seen on Narwhal,
  cray-libsci 23.05). The plain name is the right target.

## Why 2.0 and not 1.9.1

This changes the default BLAS resolution path for every Linux build, not just
Cray ones. The per-machine files in #26/#28 are the conservative fix for the
patch line; this is the one that scales to Cray EX systems we do not have
accounts on yet.

## Verification available

The four configs this would replace are each verified at 539 passed / 0 failed
/ 0 skipped on their machine, so there is a concrete baseline to check a
`default.py` implementation against. Build recipes and environment manifests:
https://github.com/cekees/proteus-modules

issues.title: proteus.richards.ADR is unimportable: richards.cADR extension not built
issues.body:
`proteus/richards/ADR.py` does `from .cADR import *`, but `setup.py` has no `richards.cADR` Extension. Only the top-level `cADR` (from `proteus/ADR.cpp`) and `richards.cRichards` are built. The source `proteus/richards/cADR.cpp` (pybind11 module `cADR`, plus `richards/ADR.h`) is tracked but never compiled, so:

- `import proteus.richards.ADR` fails with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'proteus.richards.cADR'` (after cekees/proteus#41 / cekees/proteus#42 remove the `past` import that currently fails first).
- `from proteus.richards import *` fails the same way, because `proteus/richards/__init__.py` lists `"ADR"` and `"cADR"` in `__all__`.
- Affects 1.9.0 (48f54a60), the 1.9.x branch and main.

### How it was lost
The entry existed: 079a0b46 (2024-05-22, "Adding skeleton of new ADR module") added it, and def545dd (2024-06-03) still had it. It was dropped in merge **9e2aca55** (2026-08-12, "Merge origin/add_adr into torino_narwhal_dswe_mike_qbc_jim_merged"). That merge took `setup.py` from the first parent (d6ad6791, which had no entry) over the `add_adr` side (1007d452, which did).

### Existing partial fix
Branch `docfix-sphinx-warnings` (3dac55e1, no PR yet) re-adds the Extension, mirroring `richards.cRichards`. Two things to fix before it merges:
- Its comment and commit message say the entry "never" existed; it did, see above.
- It adds `future` to `environment-dev-up.yml` for `past.utils.old_div`. cekees/proteus#41 / cekees/proteus#42 replace `old_div` with `/`, so that addition should be dropped.

### To do
1. Restore the `richards.cADR` Extension, either from `docfix-sphinx-warnings` or the 2024 form, which also had `include_dirs=['proteus/richards'] + get_xtensor_include()`.
2. Check that `richards/ADR.h` still compiles against the current `CompKernel.h`/`ArgumentsDict.h`. It hasn't been built in this tree since the August merge.
3. Add a test that at least imports `proteus.richards.ADR`. Right now only `test/richards/adr_1d_p.py` references it, and no test runs that file, which is how this went unnoticed.
4. Or, if `richards.ADR` is superseded by `proteus.ADR` / `mprans.ADR`, remove it and drop `"ADR"`/`"cADR"` from `proteus/richards/__init__.py`'s `__all__` instead.

Found while reviewing spack/spack-packages#6000 (`py-future` dependency).

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

comments.body:
Update: cekees/proteus#43 restores the Extension on 1.9.x. `richards/cADR.cpp` compiles against current headers (clang 21 / libc++), and with it built, `import proteus.richards.ADR` works.

It does **not** run yet. Running `test/richards/adr_1d_{p,n}.py` through it:
1. `getResidual` fails at `ADR.py:1160` because `argsDict["elementMaterialTypes"] = self.mesh.elementMaterialTypes,` has a trailing comma, which makes the value a tuple. The same line appears at 1341 and 1587.
2. With those fixed, it fails next because `argsDict["delta_x_ij"]` is `None`.

So item 2 of the to-do list is fine (it compiles). What remains is finishing or removing the module (items 3/4).
